idiom_name: proc-returning methods plus a bounce loop (or a small Enumerator driver)
implementation_notes: Ruby has no guaranteed tail-call elimination: the VM exposes an experimental :tailcall_optimization compile option through RubyVM::InstructionSequence.compile_option, it is not part of ordinary method compilation, and it cannot help mutual recursion anyway. The idiomatic answer is the bounce loop - the mutually recursive methods return procs instead of calling each other and a small driver keeps calling procs until a value appears - optionally wrapped in an Enumerator when the steps should be lazily produced. Blocks and procs make the step value free of ceremony, so this reads almost like direct recursion. Keep it for data-driven depth; bounded recursion stays as ordinary methods.
pitfalls: respond_to?(:call) is true for many objects that are legitimate payloads, so a callable result must be wrapped in a tagged step to avoid an endless bounce.
Blocks capture their surrounding bindings; a proc returned from a step keeps those objects alive, so long chains delay garbage collection of intermediate state.
The VM tailcall option has to be enabled for a specific instruction sequence at compile time, so code relying on it silently loses the optimisation when compiled elsewhere.
